title: Ayodhya
wiki_lead:
Ayodhya (Hindi: Ayodhyā, pronounced [ɐˈjoːd̪ʱjɐː] ) is a city situated on the banks of the Saryu river in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. It is the administrative headquarters of the Ayodhya district as well as the Ayodhya division of Uttar Pradesh, India. Ayodhya became the top tourist destination of Uttar Pradesh with 110 million visitors in the first half of 2024, surpassing Varanasi.
The settlement was historically known as Sāketa until it was renamed to Ayodhya during the Gupta period. The early Buddhist and Jain canonical texts mention that the religious leaders Gautama Buddha and Mahavira visited and lived in the city. The Jain texts also describe it as the birthplace of five tirthankaras namely, Rishabhanatha, Ajitanatha, Abhinandananatha, Sumatinatha and Anantanatha, and associate it with the legendary Bharata Chakravarti. From the Gupta period onwards, several sources mention Ayodhya and Saketa as the name of the same city.
The legendary city of Ayodhya, popularly identified as the present-day Ayodhya, is identified in the epic Ramayana and its many versions as the birthplace of the Hindu deity Rama of Kosala and is hence regarded as the first of the seven most important pilgrimage sites for Hindus. A 2nd-century CE stone slab inscription recovered from nearby Kaushambi contains a Brahmi dedicatory epigraph invoking the worship of Bhagavat Rama-Narayana, providing early epigraphic evidence of the deification of Rama within the regional Vaishnavism tradition during the Kushan period. Hans T. Bakker also notes that the earliest attestation to a place called Ayodhya is from the 2nd century CE.
The Ayodhya dispute was centred on the Babri mosque, built 1528–29 under the Mughal emperor Babur and said to have been built on top of a Hindu temple that stood at the birth spot of Rama. In 1992 a Hindu mob demolished the mosque, provoking riots throughout the country. In 2019, the Supreme Court of India announced the final verdict that the land belonged to the government based on tax records; It further ordered the land to be handed over to a trust to build the Ram Mandir; which was consecrated in January 2024. It also ordered the government to give an alternate five acre tract of land to the Uttar Pradesh Sunni Central Waqf Board to build the mosque.

Etymology
The word "Ayodhya" is a regularly formed derivation of the Sanskrit verb yudh, "to fight, or wage war". Yodhya is the future passive participle, meaning "to be fought"; the initial a is the negative prefix; the whole, therefore, means "not to be fought" or, more idiomatically in English, "invincible". This meaning is attested by the Atharvaveda, which uses it to refer to the unconquerable city of gods. The ninth century Jain poem Adi Purana also states that Ayodhya "does not exist by name alone but by the merit" of being unconquerable by enemies. Satyopakhyana interprets the word differently, stating that it means "that which cannot be conquered by sins" (instead of enemies).

Historically identified with Saketa and known as Vinita in Jain literature, it is associated with the kingdom of Kosala and the Ikshvaku dynasty and holds particular significance in Hinduism and Jainism. Archaeological evidence, including inscriptions such as that of Dhanadeva from the 1st century BCE and coins issued by local rulers like the Mitras, attests to its continuous habitation and political significance as Saketa, the early capital of Kosala, from at least the post-Mauryan period onward. In Hindu tradition, Ayodhya is revered as the capital of Kosala and the birthplace of Rama, the seventh avatar of Vishnu and central figure of the Ramayana, who is traditionally believed to have ruled the city as an ideal monarch; it is counted among Hinduism's seven sacred cities ( Sapta Puri). In Jainism, Ayodhya is regarded as the birthplace of five Tirthankaras: Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), Ajitanatha, Abhinandananatha, Sumatinatha, and Anantanatha. According to Jain tradition, Rishabhanatha established the Ikshvaku lineage and is credited with introducing agriculture, commerce, crafts, and organized social institutions; his eldest son, Bharata Chakravarti, is described as the first universal monarch of the present cosmic cycle, from whom the name Bharatvarsha is traditionally derived in Jain accounts. Ayodhya's modern history includes the Ram JanmabhoomiâBabri Masjid dispute. A mosque known as Babri Masjid was constructed in the early 16th century by Mughal general Mir Baqi; excavations conducted by the Archaeological Survey of India in 2003 revealed substantial remains of a pre-existing large structure with features characteristic of a 12th-century Hindu temple beneath the mosque's central dome, including pillars and artifacts indicating prior non-Islamic religious use. This evidence, combined with historical records of uninterrupted Hindu worship at the site, informed the Supreme Court of India's 2019 verdict, which ruled that the plaintiffs representing the Hindu community held superior title to the disputed 2.77-acre plot and directed its allocation for the construction of a Ram temple while providing an alternative site for a mosque. The Ram Mandir, a sandstone structure designed in the Nagara style, was consecrated and opened to the public on January 22, 2024, by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Beyond this modern history, Ayodhya remains a major pilgrimage centre, containing Hindu and Jain temples such as Hanuman Garhi and Kanak Bhawan, historic shrines, and sacred ghats along the Sarayu River. Following the 2024 consecration of the Ram Mandir, the city has seen infrastructure development including a new airport and railway enhancements to accommodate growing visitation, underscoring its enduring religious and cultural heritage also recognized in Buddhist traditions.
